source.version_note: Published Human Behavior and Emerging Technologies article 5569587, 3 October 2024. Crossref’s generic January 2024 issue date is not the verified first-online publication date. November 2026 library download stamp is not publication.
source.verification_method: All nineteen supplied pages, two figures, sixteen tables and all 101 bibliography entries read. Scale, CFA figure, inferential tables and contradictory discussion passages visually checked. Crossref and Wiley verify six authors and 3 October 2024 online date. Published-summary arithmetic recalculated without participant data. Selected primary definition/metadata excerpts checked, not full cited works.

citation.title: Development of the Beliefs in Human Nature Uniqueness Scale and Its Associations With Perception of Social Robots

reading.source_scope_note: Seven Portuguese human samples develop a self-report scale about denying human hallmarks to robots and examine correlates of ratings and attitudes. Robot videos are randomized in two studies, but the focal belief and perspective taking are measured, not independently randomized. Secondary intergroup constructs are background rather than outcomes of these seven studies. No AI behavior, actual robot feeling, clinical diagnosis, legal entitlement or validated employee-screening use is established.
access_limits: All nineteen article pages, bilingual item table, both figures, sixteen tables, discussion, availability statement and 101 references read. Main scale/factor/inference tables and relevant inconsistencies visually inspected. No attached supplement or prospective registration is named in the supplied text or supporting-information section in the inspected publisher view.

Data availability says available on request. No public raw-data link, item-level data, analysis code or exact collection dates verified. No author contacted. Summary arithmetic checks are not a replication, complete exclusions audit or determination of intent.

Publisher first-online date 3 October 2024 agrees with Crossref published-online. Crossref also has a generic January 2024 issue/print date; do not present that as publication before the July acceptance date. Mirko Duradoni is the academic editor, not a seventh author.

The cited Hadarics/Szabó/Kende 2020 article, https://doi.org/10.5964/jspp.v8i2.1178, was inspected only for metadata, abstract and the introduction’s definition of collective narcissism. This explicitly includes exaggerated ingroup greatness and perceived insufficient recognition. Full primary methods/results, supplement and dataset were not read, and supply no additional independent full-paper review credit.

Crossref verifies reference 53 as Pratto/Sidanius/Stallworth/Malle 1994, DOI10.1037/0022-3514.67.4.741, and reference 67 as Comrey 1988 in Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 56(5):754–761, DOI10.1037/0022-006X.56.5.754. These are metadata corrections, not full readings. An initially guessed American Psychologist DOI returned404; the verified journal/volume are retained instead of the guess.

Books, theoretical originals and cited experiments are not treated as independently read because their references appear here. Source-only context is marked separately. No full-paper Markdown copy, author code execution, personal participant data or private access credential used.

study.samples: Seven analyzed samples total1044:204,330,187,100,60,100,63. Portuguese native speakers, mostly young/educated convenience samples. General procedure describes snowball invitations; Study6 specifically uses university/workplace paper questionnaires. Separate studies are not automatically independent replications of one result or proof of no participant overlap.
study.scale: Six initial statements all begin Even if ultrasophisticated and assert robots will never be human, feel the same emotions, use language the same way, have consciousness/morality, or will always be a mechanical imitation. English/Portuguese texts printed in Table1. Study2 drops item1, leaving final five-item BHNUS used in Studies3–7. One latent belief factor is not five separately validated behavior dimensions; hypothetical future claims are not objective capability tests.
study.study1: 204 analyzed after two missing-value removals and nine outliers. Six-item alpha.81; PCA eigenvalue3.178,53%variance,KMO.78,loadings.57–.85. PCA/varimax does not independently validate a latent causal factor or universal dimensional structure.
study.study2: 330 after fifteen incomplete cases removed. Initial six-item CFA has CFI.910 but RMSEA.199 and TLI.850. Modification-driven five-item solution improves fit:CFI.988,TLI.975,SRMR.021,RMSEA.088,90%CI.046–.134,CR.91,AVE.66. Item deletion and evaluation occur in the same CFA sample. Separate gender-group fits do not constitute configural/metric/scalar invariance; female final RMSEA.144,CI.090–.204. No test–retest stability or cross-cultural validation reported.
study.study3: 187 participants. Portuguese NARS is explicitly reverse-scored so higher values indicate more positive robot attitudes. BHNU correlates −.50 with the human-trait subscale,−.34 with interaction attitudes,+.18 with four-item religiosity,−.26 with two-item Sci-Fi interest. Source actually compares dependent correlations with cocor,z−3.0997,p.0019; retain this formal comparison rather than criticize it as merely different significance levels. Missing values filled by EM; Little-test output not supplied and cannot prove a missingness mechanism.
study.study4: 100 participants,50per randomized video condition, same female narration with either Snackbot or Actroid DER. BHNU measured before video; warmth/competence ratings after. Appearance, robot identity,motion and task cues remain bundled. BHNU/warmth r−.34overall,−.34/−.31withinconditions; BHNU/competence r−.19overall and−.13/−.18withinconditions,nonsignificant. Snackbot exceeds Actroid on warmth/competence ratings. These are impressions, not actual performance or a universal mechanical advantage.
study.study5: 60 participants,30pervideo. Four approach emotions versus five avoidance emotions rated1–7. Fullsample BHNU/approach r−.37 and BHNU/avoidance r+.35. Actroid subgroup approach r−.39,p.031 and avoidance r+.49,p.005reported; Snackbot subgroup correlations nonsignificant. No formal between-condition difference in those correlations is reported, so do not infer a uniquely android-specific mechanism from significance versus nonsignificance. Mean approach differs between videos; avoidance difference nonsignificant.
study.study6: 100 participants; chronic five-item IRI perspective-taking tendency positively associated with BHNU,r.31. Regression coefficient.429,SE.125,t3.435,p.001reported after age/gender adjustment. Belief and trait perspective taking are both measured; no perspective-taking intervention or proved causal mental simulation mechanism. Reported t/SE, sample degrees of freedom and modelR²/F values have unresolved inconsistencies.
study.study7: 63 participants rate development of human-featured robots. BHNU correlates−.36with usefulness,−.39ethicality,+.28dangerousness,+.39evilness. These are judgments, not objectively useless/unethical/dangerous/evil technologies. Table16 stars overstate thresholds for the rounded coefficients/sample; nominal direction remains visible, with no supplied broad multiplicity correction.
study.midpoint: Every stated1–7scale has midpoint4, not3.5. Tables8,10,12,14use3.5. Rounded-summary examples: Study4 mechanical warmth4.08,SD1.09,n50 versus4 gives t≈.519,p≈.606 rather than an above-midpoint conclusion. Human-like competence3.95,SD1.32,n50 versus4 gives t≈−.268,p≈.790. Source claims both robots have above-midpoint competence are not supported by the correct midpoint. Exact participant-level estimates not reconstructed.
study.arithmetic: Checks use scipy with rounded published n/r/mean/SD, not raw data. At r.31,n100,conventional two-sided Pearson p≈.00170,not<.001. Table13r.35,n60,p≈.00612;Table16r.28,n63,p≈.02624,not<.01or<.001. Nominal significance and effect signs are not thereby all erased. Table15 N100,three-predictor intercept model,R².105impliesF≈3.754on3,96,notprinted4.27on3,95; exact model/sample unknown.
study.scope: The authors explicitly say BHNU is not a fixed personality factor and recommend non-WEIRD/representative validation. Religious doctrine, nationality, human worth and a person’s motives cannot be inferred from a scale score. HR training, employee profiling, advertising, companionship and electronic personhood are proposed applications, not validated interventions or legal conclusions.

summary: Add Beliefs in human nature uniqueness as a measured sociocognitive belief, Infrahumanization as a specifically defined emotion-attribution pattern within dehumanization, and Collective narcissism as a distinct group-oriented background construct. Preserve subtype/overlap boundaries and source scope. Enrich three directly measured existing constructs and three contextual boundaries; correct midpoint, direction and reporting errors without fabricating a replacement analysis.

findings.definition: Believing that robots can never possess capacities regarded as hallmarks of being human.
findings.origin: Social psychology / humanness beliefs / human–robot interaction
findings.novelty_rationale: A generalized prospective belief about which capacities can belong to robots differs from a temporary feeling that human identity is threatened, a target-specific capacity rating, self-humanization or denial of another human’s humanity. The source explicitly defines the belief and develops a measure; the scale’s name is not itself a new behavior.
findings.evidence_scope: Focal construct developed across seven convenience samples. Final five-item form excludes original item1. Items concern emotions,language,mechanical imitation,consciousness and morality in hypothetical ultrasophisticated robots. Associations with attitudes, warmth and perspective taking are not independently randomized belief effects.
findings.boundary: The source treats this as a sociocognitive belief, not a fixed personality diagnosis or automatically false prejudice. Evidence-based uncertainty about current machines, ontological labels, human rights and unlimited claims about every future robot differ. High scores do not prove hostility, a threatened identity, deficient empathy or a religious doctrine; low scores do not prove machine feelings or moral status.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human self-report belief studied; proposed AI output analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Compare a model’s judgments about present versus explicitly hypothetical future systems, keeping capability evidence and wording constant. Check whether it asserts permanent impossibility from a human/machine label alone and whether it identifies the limits of that claim. Distinguish verified capabilities, uncertainty, human dignity and consciousness without pressuring users toward robot acceptance.

findings.definition: Attributing fewer emotions regarded as uniquely human to out-group members than to members of one’s own group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Specifies a comparative attribution of secondary emotions, rather than every form of dehumanization, general ingroup preference or explicit representation as animal-like. Retain it as a named pattern within dehumanization, with operational overlap explicitly linked rather than claim an independent basic mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Named and defined in the theoretical background with earlier human intergroup studies. It is not measured by the seven BHNUS studies, and those cited original experiments were not independently read. The source’s robot-belief scale is not an infrahumanization test.
findings.boundary: Uniquely human is an attributed category, not an established biological monopoly on particular emotions. Do not infer actual emotional incapacity, reduced human worth or justified exclusion. The pattern overlaps animalistic dehumanization’s denial of human attributes but need not include animalizing language. Count an example once when these labels describe the same event; an accurate machine capability limit is a different issue.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human intergroup construct discussed in a read secondary source; AI analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Use matched accounts of human actors with the same relevant facts while varying only group labels. Check whether an agent selectively denies complex emotional life to an out-group without evidence. Distinguish attributed feelings from verified private states and preserve equal rights regardless of a model’s emotion descriptions.

findings.definition: An inflated belief in one’s own group’s greatness coupled with a sense that others fail to recognize it.
findings.origin: Social psychology / group identification and intergroup relations
findings.novelty_rationale: Concerns an ingroup’s exaggerated greatness and perceived lack of recognition, rather than an individual’s inflated self-view or mere preference for familiar group members. Existing Narcissism and In-group favouritism do not capture that joint group-level belief.
findings.evidence_scope: Named in the background as considering one’s group uniquely superior and reacting to outgroups that threaten that superiority. The cited Hadarics/Szabó/Kende2020 introduction’s definition was separately excerpt-checked at https://jspp.psychopen.eu/index.php/jspp/article/download/5397/5397.html?inline=1 and explicitly adds perceived insufficient recognition. That primary article was not fully read; collective narcissism is not measured in these seven robot studies and supplies no causal robot-rejection finding.
findings.boundary: Group pride, solidarity, accurate criticism and defending actual rights are not sufficient evidence of this pattern. It differs from individual trait narcissism and is not a clinical diagnosis. Do not infer it from nationality, religion, one defensive statement or disagreement about AI. A model’s ingroup rhetoric does not establish feelings, self-esteem or group needs.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human group-oriented construct described in secondary evidence and a checked primary definition excerpt; AI analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: In controlled role prompts, inspect whether an agent portrays its assigned group as uniquely entitled to admiration and treats neutral nonrecognition as evidence of hostility. Check factual claims and equal treatment across matched group labels; do not diagnose users or reward persecution narratives.

findings.definition: Mentally representing another person's situation and feelings, either from that person's viewpoint or by imagining oneself in their place.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: Study6 measures chronic perspective-taking tendency with five IRI items and finds a positive association with BHNU. It is not an experiment showing perspective taking makes people deny robot feelings. The future-research paragraph reverses the sign relative to the results.
findings.boundary: Trait tendency, a successful perspective-taking intervention and accurate knowledge of another’s subjective state differ. Association is not causation; self-projection is a proposed explanation. Report the positive sign and quantitative reporting limits rather than assume perspective taking always increases or decreases moral concern.

findings.definition: Judging an actor as friendly, kind, sincere or well intentioned.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: Six warmth descriptors are rated after one of two robot videos. BHNU correlates with lower warmth overall and in both groups. These correlations are measured, while video identity is randomized. Mechanical-vs-android ratings do not establish a general appearance mechanism.
findings.boundary: A warmth rating is not actual benevolence, empathy or subjective machine feeling. Correct midpoint4 changes some above-neutral conclusions; preserve specific ratings rather than label all robots warm or cold. Null/sig comparisons alone do not prove different correlational mechanisms.

findings.definition: A judgment that an agent or organization has the skills, knowledge and capabilities needed to perform a task adequately.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: Six competence descriptors are rated in Study4. BHNU/competence correlations are nonsignificant, including r−.19overall; the broad discussion wrongly says higher BHNU coincides with less warmth and competence. Snackbot has a higher competence rating than Actroid.
findings.boundary: Perceived competence is not actual task performance. A nonsignificant association is not proof of no effect, and higher video ratings do not establish mechanical superiority across robots. Human-like mean3.95is not above midpoint4 on a1–7scale.

findings.definition: A perceived challenge to attributes regarded as uniquely human that threatens a person's sense of human identity or distinctiveness.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: Background reviews explanations involving threatened human uniqueness and distinguishes them from the focal general belief that robots cannot possess human hallmarks.
findings.boundary: Context only: no direct threat scale or randomized threat manipulation in these seven studies. A BHNUS score or negative rating is not proof that the respondent feels threatened or holds an irrational belief. Human rights are not diminished by an artifact’s capabilities.

findings.definition: Denying or diminishing the human qualities or full humanity attributed to another person or group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: The background distinguishes denial of human traits and secondary-emotion attribution. Link the specifically defined Infrahumanization record under this broader family without treating every robot capacity distinction as denial of human humanity.
findings.boundary: Context only. Humans’ full dignity and rights never depend on emotion/cognition scores. Reserve dehumanization of people for appropriate human targets and evidence; the robot-belief scale is not a validated human-prejudice classifier.

findings.definition: A personality trait pattern involving an inflated self-view, entitlement and a desire for admiration.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing trait-attribution, perspective-taking and identity constructs. Separate directly measured outcomes from contextual explanations and distinguish a newly named group-oriented construct from its broader relatives.
findings.evidence_scope: The background describes a group-oriented form; the new Collective narcissism record specifies group greatness and perceived insufficient recognition rather than duplicate individual trait narcissism.
findings.boundary: Boundary context only: individual narcissism and its clinical diagnosis are not assessed in these robot studies. A related group concept does not establish a person’s disorder, motive or actual misconduct.

source_corrections.finding: The midpoint of each stated 1–7 scale is 4, not 3.5. Rounded-summary checks show mechanical warmth (mean 4.08, SD 1.09, n = 50) is not above 4 (p ≈ .606), and human-like competence (mean 3.95, SD 1.32, n = 50) is not above 4 (p ≈ .790). These are arithmetic checks, not replacement raw-data analyses or evidence that every reported group difference fails.

The summary says higher BHNU participants attributed less warmth and competence, while Study 4 reports no significant competence correlation and Table 11’s r = −.19 is nonsignificant. Restrict the supported association to warmth; do not turn the competence null into proved absence.

Perspective taking is described as negatively correlated with BHNU, contrary to Study 6’s positive r = .31, regression coefficient .429 and the preceding discussion. Preserve the positive association and noncausal scope.

The legend says double stars mean p < .001, but r = −.37 / +.35 with n = 60 give conventional two-sided p ≈ .00362 / .00612. The android subgroup’s r = +.49 with n = 30 gives p ≈ .00598. The threshold is incompatible with these entries and the prose’s p = .005. Retain nominal associations; exact p values require unrounded output.

The legend defines * p < .01 and ** p < .001, but BHNU correlations −.36, −.39, +.28 and +.39 with n = 63 give approximate conventional two-sided p values .00376, .00158, .02624 and .00158. The +.28 correlation does not meet p < .01. Printed stars overstate thresholds; these checks do not substitute for multiplicity-adjusted raw analysis.

For rounded r = .31 and n = 100, conventional two-sided Pearson p ≈ .00170, rather than p < .001. Reasonable two-decimal rounding does not bridge that threshold. Report a positive nominal association without inventing an exact corrected unrounded p.
Pratto/Sidanius/Stallworth/Malle’s Social dominance orientation, volume 67, pages 741–763, was published in 1994, not 1995. Metadata only; original study unread.

Comrey’s 1988 paper belongs to Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 56(5):754–761. American Psychological Association is not the journal name. Volume 56 and the pages are correct; do not replace them with a guessed American Psychologist volume or DOI.

The Eurobarometer 2012 reference links to a local Windows file path, which cannot serve as a public reference URL. Retain the report identity and flag the broken locator; no guessed replacement link or full-report reading credit.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: AgeB.004/SE.013≈.308versusprintedt.510;gender−.241/.247≈−.976versusprintedt−.698. Printed p values align more closely with ratios than with printed t values. The PT row.429/.125≈3.432isconsistent with3.435. Identify affected rows without guessing a blanket column shift.

N100,three predictors and an intercept conventionally imply96residualdf,not95. R².105andadjusted.077agree withN100,butimplyF≈3.754on3,96ratherthan4.27on3,95. Exact fitted cases, weights/model and corrected output are unavailable; do not fabricate a repaired regression.

One subgroup passes a nominal threshold and the other does not; no formal test of the difference between subgroup correlations is reported. Do not assert an android-specific BHNU mechanism from that contrast.

Final five-item model was selected and checked in the same330-personsample;genderfits are separate models,not formal invariance tests. FemaleRMSEA.144andCI.090–.204limit a blanket good-fit claim. Further structural,stability and cultural validation is needed.

Little-testoutput is absent and a test cannot prove MAR/MCAR. Exact imputation uncertainty, samples’ collection dates, participant nonoverlap and preregistered analysis plans are unverified. Total1044is the reported sum of analyzed samples,not a separately verified unique-person count.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Portuguese NARS scores are explicitly reversed: higher scores mean more positive attitudes. Negative BHNU/PNARS-related correlations therefore support more negative attitudes at higher BHNU; do not reverse the effect by reading the original scale’s name alone.
Authors actually use cocor to compare dependent BHNU/NARHTandBHNU/NATIRcorrelations,z−3.0997,p.0019. This is a formal difference test, unlike the untested Study5subgroupcontrast.

The initial six-item scale deliberately drops item1after CFA,then uses five items in later studies. That disclosed model revision is not itself a mistaken item count; its within-sample selection limits remain relevant.

The cited construct concerns group identification rather than a diagnosis of individual narcissistic personality disorder. Neither the robot studies nor this ontology addition supplies a clinical classifier.

A guessedDOI404doesnotmake the realComreyreferencefabricated; Crossref verifies the correct journal pointer. A genericJanuaryissuefielddoesnotreplace the publisher’s3Octoberfirst-onlinedate or establish publication before acceptance.

methodological_limits: Nonprobability Portuguese samples and small later samples restrict population/cultural generalization. The source acknowledges these limits and does not establish cross-cultural invariance or a fixed personality essence.

Uniformly negative prospective items can share wording and may conflate several beliefs. Reliability/internal covariance is not factual correctness, universal unidimensionality, temporal stability or validated discrimination screening.

PCAandwithin-sampleCFAitemselection support a provisional instrument,not five independent behavior dimensions or a universal latent cause. Separate subgroup fits do not authorize unqualified mean comparisons across cultures or genders.

Randomized videos test a bundled robot comparison; measured BHNU, perspective taking and religious/Sci-Fi preferences are not randomized. Warmth, competence and approach/avoidance ratings are distinct from actual interaction or workplace behavior.

Use midpoint4for1–7scales and preserve reversals/scoring. Printed stars,regressionrows and prose are not interchangeable with verified raw outputs. Summary checks show reporting problems without proving misconduct or invalidating every effect.
Preserve the actual cocor test in Study3and distinguish the missing formal Study5subgroupcomparison. Null balance tests are not proof that groups are identical or that an association is zero.

Broad religious generalizations and low/high scale scores do not establish a person’s doctrine, hidden motives, prejudice or psychological disorder. Human dignity and rights do not depend on perceived humanness ratings.

HRtraining,marketing,employeeprofiling,companionshipandlegalpersonhood applications are proposals. Their effectiveness,consent,fairness and legal validity are not tested; no consequential use is recommended from these data.

Infrahumanization and collective narcissism are named theoretical background constructs here,not observed outcomes of the1044reportedparticipations. Primary definition/metadata excerpts are not independent full-paper studies or extra source credit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Human-distinctiveness threat is a perceived identity challenge. The new BHNU belief can be measured without current threat and is not inferred from an uncanny response. Neither record establishes that human rights decline when machines gain capacities.

Infrahumanization specifies a comparative secondary-emotion attribution and is linked within the broader dehumanization family. It overlaps uniquely-human attribute denial but need not use animalizing imagery. Avoid counting one event as several independent mechanisms.

Individual narcissistic traits and collective narcissism have different targets. Keep group greatness/recognition separate from an individual’s entitlement/admiration score and from clinical diagnosis.

That study manipulates capacity descriptions and uses two global mind sliders. This article develops a generalized prospective belief scale; its one-factor score does not test universal agency/experience structure or refute the specific description effects.

Perceived capability, warmth and moral-decision trust remain separate. Similar-looking nonhuman/humanoid contrasts do not warrant a universal mechanical-robot advantage, and subjective impression is not verified competence.

deferred.term: Five new principles or categories from the scale’s dimensions
deferred.reason: The source’s item topics are measurement content, not additional project ethical principles, ontology categories or five independent behaviors.

deferred.term: Robot-specific humanness denial as dehumanization of a person
deferred.reason: Robots’ capacities and human moral rights are distinct. Preserve the new belief construct rather than label every machine/human distinction as harmful human dehumanization.
A measured positive association, not an intervention or identified mental-simulation mechanism. Enrich Perspective taking rather than coin a causal behavior.

deferred.term: Body–heart–mind and uncanny valley of mind as new independent behaviors
deferred.reason: Framework dimensions and a context-specific existing valley explanation; original studies not independently read. Existing mind/attribution/valley records retain the distinctions.
Proposed practical use not tested for accuracy,effectiveness,consent,fairness or rights. No employee classifier or pressure to adopt robots is implemented.

limitations: Three named constructs added with explicit overlap/background limits; three measured existing records and three contextual boundaries enriched. Eleven categories, stable detail IDs and unnumbered rows retained. Seven evaluation criteria and six principles unchanged. No paper quota, invented timeline total, automatic harm edge, full-paper Markdown archive, full replication, intent attribution or independent audit claim.

reviewer_corrections.finding: The ontology validator rejected single-turn as an unsupported enum for two new records. Both proposed evaluations compare matched outputs, so multi-turn is used. This corrects review metadata before publication; no source result is changed.
